barriers.description: COVID-19 restrictions forced all interviews to be conducted remotely via Zoom, biasing participation toward technologically literate stakeholders and limiting in-person engagement.
barriers.justification: Remote-only interviews constrained the designers' ability to facilitate broad user involvement and to understand context of use through in-person observation, reducing the representativeness of user understanding and potentially limiting requirements specification and iteration.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Because of ongoing COVID-19 restrictions on in-person engagements, interviews were conducted via the UCSF Zoom video platform (Zoom Video Communications, Inc) ... All interviews were conducted remotely, using the UCSF Zoom video platform, which may have biased the patient stakeholders to people who are technologically literate and have access to the internet.

barriers.description: Qualitative analysis was conducted with the interviewer serving as the sole coder, introducing risk of analytic bias in interpreting stakeholder feedback.
barriers.justification: Relying on a single coder impeded the team's ability to robustly synthesize and triangulate user insights, which hinders managing user understanding, integrating feedback and iteration, and specifying reliable user requirements.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Although the interviewer was the sole coder, the stakeholder advisory team provided ongoing consultation on the coding scheme and how to code less frequently occurring responses. Finally, having the interviewer serve as the primary coder could have introduced bias into the qualitative analysis process.

barriers.description: Participant sampling was limited to clinicians at UCSF and patients seen by that group, which may have omitted important feedback from a wider cohort of users.
barriers.justification: This recruitment scope constrained designers' ability to manage user understanding and validate generalizability, limiting their capacity to specify requirements and ensure the tool fits diverse contexts of use.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Only clinicians at UCSF and patients seen by this (broad) group of clinicians were interviewed; therefore, we may have missed important feedback from a wider cohort of users.

barriers.description: Integration and scalability of the tool to other health systems depended on each system's internal governance and motivation, posing an external organizational constraint.
barriers.justification: This external dependence limited the designers' ability to plan and execute scalable implementations and to coordinate multidisciplinary adoption across health systems, hindering the operational workload of producing deployable solutions and integrating them into varied clinical workflows.
barriers.reference_excerpt: However, successful integration into other health systems depends on the internal governance and motivation within each system.

barriers.description: Collected wearable data are largely inaccessible for visualization or integration within clinic EHRs, limiting availability of patient-generated data streams.
barriers.justification: Inaccessible wearable data prevented designers from integrating important data sources into the tool, constraining their ability to specify requirements, produce design solutions that incorporate multimodal PGD, and evaluate designs with realistic data inputs.
barriers.reference_excerpt: However, most of the collected wearable data remain inaccessible for visualization or integration within a clinic’s EHR. This limitation can impede the effective use of PGD by clinicians and compromise patient-physician collaboration related to PGD [52].
